claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is single-phase.
The initial alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
Relatively low deformation temperature combined with high strain rate induces elemental segregation at grain boundaries.
The deformation-induced grain-boundary segregation is localized to certain alloying elements.
At low temperature and high strain rate, insufficient dislocation movement prevents uniform atomic redistribution and thereby causes grain-boundary segregation.
Segregated grain boundaries have reduced local cohesive strength.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion promotes brittle, often intergranular, failure.
Increasing deformation temperature and decreasing strain rate cause the segregation to disappear.
The disappearance of segregation at higher temperature or lower strain rate is attributable to enhanced dislocation movement.
Higher-temperature or lower-strain-rate deformation preserves ductility and produces predominantly transgranular failure.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate deformation should produce more grain-boundary segregation than high-temperature, low-strain-rate deformation.
The increase in grain-boundary segregation should correlate with a shift toward brittle intergranular fracture.
The as-sintered or as-cast baseline exhibits homogeneous composition.
The as-sintered or as-cast baseline exhibits ductile transgranular fracture under moderate deformation.
Grain-boundary morphology, including serration, can materially affect deformation localization and ductility.
The proposed mechanism is limited to conditions without transformation to a multiphase structure or formation of deleterious intermetallic phases.
